title: Farmer Collecting Cattle Fodder Mauled to Death by Tiger in Beed, Maharashtra
excerpt: Devidas (Mahadev) Takle of Deolali village in Ashti tehsil was killed on Saturday while collecting fodder for his cattle in drought-hit Maharashtra, in an attack reports link to a young male tiger camera-trapped in the area on November 2.
body:
• A farmer was mauled to death by a tiger while collecting fodder for his cattle in Maharashtra's Beed district on Saturday, November 7, 2026.
  • The victim was identified as Devidas (Mahadev) Takle, a resident of Deolali village in Ashti tehsil.
  • Reports say forest camera traps had captured the same male tiger inside the Ashti forest boundary on November 2, and the forest department had issued safety advisories after that sighting.
  • Forest officials say patrols and camera monitoring have been increased and are urging farmers to avoid forested and hilly areas — the practical instruction for villages around Ashti and Patoda.

A farmer was mauled to death by a tiger while collecting fodder for his cattle in Maharashtra's Beed district on Saturday, in an incident that has sparked fresh anger among villagers over repeated big-cat attacks in the region. The victim was identified as Devidas (Mahadev) Takle, a resident of Deolali village in Ashti tehsil, according to India Today.

What the reports say happened

Takle was cutting fodder on a hillside near Deolali when the tiger attacked, and officials confirmed the animal dragged him into dense thorn scrub before fleeing, according to Particle News's synthesis of the reporting. Villagers who discovered the attack confronted the scene with sticks and axes, forcing the tiger to abandon the body and retreat into deep forest, and local leaders are demanding capture or stronger measures.

A tiger already on the department's radar

The animal is reported to be a male born in 2022 at Tipeshwar Wildlife Sanctuary to tigress T-22, which has been moving frequently across Beed district, including livestock attacks in Patoda tehsil on October 17. Forest camera traps captured the same male inside the Ashti forest boundary on November 2, and the department issued safety advisories to local residents after that sighting. Saturday's killing, while Takle was doing the routine drought-season work of gathering cattle fodder, is what turned that advisory into village anger.

What happens next

Forest officials say patrols and camera monitoring have been increased, and they urge farmers to avoid forested and hilly areas, because repeated dispersal of young male tigers raises the odds of human-wildlife conflict. For Deolali and neighbouring villages, the immediate tension is practical: fodder collection cannot simply stop in a drought-hit district, which is why villagers are pressing the department for capture or stronger protective measures rather than advisories alone.
